newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan defends slashing foreign aid budget.
newsitem.headline: Japan defends slashing foreign aid budget.

text.p: Japan's Foreign Ministry defended on Thursday its reductions in the Official Development Assistance (ODA) budget for foreign assistance.
"There has been a stereotype created of a Japan that simply opens its chequebook and disburses funds, but that is the wrong interpretation," a senior Foreign Ministry official told Reuters.
The Foreign Ministry said on Monday that Japan's foreign aid in 1996 fell 35 percent from the previous year to $9.58 billion, the lowest dollar value in six years.

In yen terms, foreign aid in 1996 had been cut by 24.8 percent to 1,042.5 billion yen ($8.27 billion), its lowest level in almost twenty years, with the ratio of ODA to gross national product plunging to 0.21 percent.

The ODA cuts came as Japan remained embroiled in a hostage crisis in Peru which has shaken public confidence in Japan's leadership and led to condemnation of what critics say are aid policies which have reinforced the image of the Japanese as being rich.
The official defended the cuts, saying Japan would concentrate on improving the quality of aid and widening the circle of aid recipients.
"Japan must shift the focus (of aid) so it is more based on quality and think of improving it by providing funds to more people in the field," he said.

A weak yen, foreign aid cuts as part of government fiscal tightening and rising repayments from developing countries on long-term loans had dragged the net dollar value of Japan's foreign aid disbursement to its lowest level since 1990, the official said.
